item.title: I almost wrote off these Galaxy One UI 9 features as gimmicks, but they genuinely made my life better
item.itunes:title: I almost wrote off these Galaxy One UI 9 features as gimmicks, but they genuinely made my life better
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Absolutely everyone with a Samsung phone seems to have something to say about the recently rolled-out One UI 9, and if you believe half the internet, Samsung has somehow managed to turn a software update into a religious experience. Everywhere I saw, people were calling new One UI 9 features "game-changing," "must-try," and downright "insane," all before anyone could've spent enough time with them to truly know if they were worth hyping up so much. I myself was firmly in the skeptical camp, I'll admit.

Then, I updated my Galaxy S25 and started using some of the new features that Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts kept drowning my algorithm in. Within a week, the features that I'd judged from screenshots and dismissed as gimmicks quietly worked their way into my daily routine. One UI 9 hasn't "reinvented" my Galaxy S25, but some of its new features have truly been making my life easier every day.

I turned my Samsung Galaxy into a speed machine by ditching Samsung's bloated launcher

The official launcher is of no good.

1
By  Anurag Singh

Quick Settings is finally as customizable as I've always wanted

One UI 9 hands me the keys to the control panel

Inarguably the biggest highlight in Samsung's new One UI 9 is the incredible amount of customizability that has now come to the Quick Settings panel. The Quick Settings panel (or Control Center) makes the life of any Android user easier every day, and One UI 9 has only made it easier. I now have more granular control over individual sections, with the ability to resize supported controls, and decide just how much screen real estate each icon or toggle deserves.

The brightness and volume sliders don't have to compete anymore with other toggles that I rarely ever touch, and I can prioritize the controls I actually use throughout the day. Initially, I dismissed this "added flexibility" as customization for customization's sake, but having my most-used controls exactly where my thumb expects them to be has genuinely made a noticeable difference in the way I use my phone.

The star of the show here is the media player, which, up until One UI 8.5, could only be resized a little bit vertically, but is now completely resizable, down to a 2x2 widget inside the Control Center. The Media Player also gets a live waveform animation for any media it's playing, and dare I say, it's gorgeous to look at. Plus, the new waveform animation for the media player makes its way outside the Control Center to the homescreen, and even the Now Bar on the lock screen.

4 launchers that turn my boring Pixel home screen into something actually useful

Give your Pixel a fresh look with these powerful launchers.

4
By  Yash Patel

I barely open the app drawer, thanks to Finder on my home screen

One less step between me and whatever I'm looking for

One of my absolute favorite features on my iPhone is the Spotlight Search, which lets me swipe down on the home screen and immediately make system-wide searches for apps, contacts, files, messages, and web results. The One UI equivalent to that on my Galaxy S25 so far had been the Finder search bar, but I had no way to directly (and quickly) bring up the Finder local search engine.

Even on One UI 8.5, I always knew the Finder existed, but accessing it still meant going through an extra step or two, at which point I could just open the File Explorer or app drawer myself. With One UI 9, I now have the Finder directly on my home screen.

All I had to do was long tap on the Home screen, tap Settings, and click on Show search on Home screen. Here, I switched on the Finder toggle, and just like that, One UI 9 put a quick Finder search right on my home screen.

Now that my phone Finder is easier to use, the feature has proven particularly useful for settings that are buried several menus deep. I no longer have to remember exact paths, since I can simply type in the name of a setting or feature and Finder will take me to it immediately.

My Samsung camera felt basic until these hidden settings unlocked its full potential

Hidden tools that changed my photography.

By  Parth Shah

I can cut unwanted apps off from the internet

AI Network Guard gives me control over which apps get to phone home

Another one of my favorite new features in One UI 9 is apparently a privacy feature. However, it has actually proved to be a rather effective productivity feature for me. AI Network Guard is a brand-new feature in One UI 9, and it can restrict internet access for specific apps you select. On paper, it's a pretty solid tool for parents if they want their kids to stay focused and not play online games.

On the other hand, though, using AI Network Guard on some of my local games has actually helped rid them of ads, since the games themselves don't need the internet. The old-school method of turning off your Wi-Fi or Mobile Data to avoid ads in games also prevented notifications from important apps, but AI Network Guard improves that method by specifically cutting off particular apps and games from the internet.

For me, cutting off particularly distracting apps like WhatsApp, Instagram, and YouTube, at least for the duration of work, has greatly helped me stay focused. Of course, I can always enter the Guardian PIN and regain access to the internet, but the friction involved is what keeps me focused.

Turning on AI Network Guard is just a teensy bit tricky though. Head to Settings > Connections > Wi-Fi. Here, tap the three-dot icon, and select Intelligent Wi-Fi. Now, click on the Intelligent Wi-Fi button seven times to unlock Connectivity labs. With Connectivity Labs open, scroll down to find and tap AI Network Guard. Once you tap on it, select Set up a Guardian PIN. Set up the PIN, and select Manage Restrictions. This is where you can select which apps you want to cut off from the internet, and press Confirm on the top-right to finalize your selections.

Find out which unexpected OneUI features are secretly draining your Galaxy phone's battery and how to disable them.

By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

Multi-finger gestures make my Galaxy a power user playground

Good Lock has helped me ditch the usual taps and swipes

I've always been a fan of shortcuts that save me from navigating menus, but multi-finger gestures initially sounded like a solution searching for a problem. By and large, the three-finger swipe down for a screenshot has been the only way I use finger-based gestures on my Galaxy S25, but One UI 9 arrived and changed that within a single week.

This new feature in One UI 9 helps me assign actions to custom gestures involving multiple fingers. As it turns out, there's indeed a method to this madness. I can configure gestures to take screenshots, toggle Dark mode, turn the screen off, increase or decrease brightness or volume, enable split-screen, and tens of other quick actions from wherever I am. Of course, the learning curve involved remembering which gesture and how many fingers I assigned to each action, but within a week, I've been using almost every quick-panel feature solely through multi-finger gestures in One UI 9.

To turn on Multi-finger gestures, you'll need the remarkably versatile Good Lock app installed. Head to Good Lock (install it through the Play Store if you don't have it). Once it's running, download the Home Up module, and select Gesture settings. Here, turn on Multi finger gesture, and tap on it to enter its customization menu. This is where you can select up to nine different actions for two, three, four, and five-finger swipe gestures for a total of thirty-six separate finger-based shortcuts, all thanks to One UI 9. Now that my muscle memory has settled, these shortcuts have become surprisingly difficult to give up.

My phone runs local LLMs faster than my gaming PC, and it's the setup I actually reach for every day

The PC wins on paper, but the phone wins in practice

19
By  Nolen Jonker

My FanCam is the Galaxy AI feature I didn't know I needed

No more manually cropping everyone out of my videos

With One UI 9, one of the honest-to-goodness new features is My FanCam, which is particularly useful for those who live in their gallery and fill it up with the camera. For any video I shoot with multiple people or subjects, My FanCam, using Galaxy AI, easily highlights a specific person through subject-focused tracking shots. The best part, of course, is that this feature gives me outputs in any aspect ratio I require, be it vertical for Instagram Reels or 4:3 videos to share in the family group chat.

To use My FanCam, all you need to do is have a video open in the Gallery app. From there, tap the Galaxy AI button in the interface, which brings up the option to select My FanCam. Highlight the person in the video you want to follow, choose an aspect ratio, and then click Follow. Within a few seconds, One UI 9 and Galaxy AI will give me a completely tracked video with my chosen person on the screen at all times. The last step, then, is to tap Save copy to reframe the video and save it locally.

In fact, the My FanCam feature even works on externally imported videos, as long as they are saved locally on my Galaxy phone and are present in the Gallery app. Since this is a post-recording AI editing tool, My FanCam doesn't care if the video it edits wasn't shot on the Galaxy phone.

I turned my old Samsung Galaxy into a $200 smart home hub, and it replaced three separate devices

It does more than I expected it to do

By  Anurag Singh

I can't believe I almost ignored these genuine upgrades

When it comes to user expectations from smartphones in 2026, we want bigger camera sensors, faster processors, brighter displays, and AI features that can apparently do everything. Meanwhile, it's the little software additions that are genuinely improving our relationship with our devices, but they rarely get the appreciation they deserve. I suppose that's what happens when a feature doesn't make for a particularly exciting launch presentation.

My experience with One UI 9 has served to remind me that I just needed better control over the wheel I already use every single day. The one thing I know for certain is that the next time a seemingly insignificant feature catches my eye, I'll give it a fair shot before dismissing it as another gimmick.

item.title: Zigbee's best feature isn't battery life, it's that the network gets stronger with every device you add
item.itunes:title: Zigbee's best feature isn't battery life, it's that the network gets stronger with every device you add
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Traditional Wi-Fi-based smart homes tend to get worse when it comes to performance as they grow. This is because adding dozens of devices bogs down your router, clogs local IP tables, and can lead to constant connection drops.

Of course, a great benefit of swapping over to Zigbee is the coin-cell sensors that last for years. True, but focusing only on battery efficiency misses the real architectural magic. Traditional networks degrade under congestion, but Zigbee operates like a living decentralized mesh. Every mains-powered device you plug into the wall acts as an active repeater, so the network mathematically improves as your smart home grows.

You're not just saving energy with Zigbee. It's an expanding architectural web. By understanding how its mesh topology leverages every new node, you realize why building a massive smart home actually makes your signal more bulletproof, not less.

Can you have too many mesh network nodes?

Mesh networks are a great way to enhance connectivity, but how many nodes is too many?

4
By  Ty Sherback

How does Zigbee mesh work?

There are three forms of Zigbee devices

The way Zigbee data moves across a home is what makes it so reliable compared to traditional Wi-Fi smart home devices. You can use a range of Zigbee devices in your home, typically divided into three subcategories: coordinators, routers, and end devices.

The central coordinator is typically your main hub. This can be a smart home hub, a Home Assistant USB dongle, or a SmartThings hub. All of your Zigbee devices communicate with this central hub, whether that's to access information from the internet or just to communicate with one another.

The next are the battery-powered end devices, like sensors. These devices typically go to sleep when they're not in use to save power. They don't actually grow and expand the mesh. That's where the unsung heroes come in: the routers. Zigbee routers are mains-powered devices like switches, smart plugs, and bulbs. item.title: Linus calls banning AI-generated code "utterly stupid" as Linux submissions no longer need LLM disclosure
item.itunes:title: Linus calls banning AI-generated code "utterly stupid" as Linux submissions no longer need LLM disclosure
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Kernel submissions no longer require the "Assisted-by" LLM disclosure.
  • Maintainers deprecated "Assisted-by" after the Prague summit; AI use no longer needs declaration.
  • Torvalds calls banning AI "utterly stupid" and insists contributors must understand their code.

There has been a big debate over the use of AI in Linux. We've seen some projects swear off the tech, saying that it's unethical to use it. We've seen some projects adopt it, claiming that it's the new frontier for programming and cannot be ignored. It has gotten to the point where if you use Linux, you're using a system that's a Frankenstein-monster-esque mix of AI submissions and strictly human-written code.

The main man himself, Linus Torvalds, has made his stance very clear in the past few months: AI coding is beneficial, here to stay, and even makes programming fun. Now, the Linux maintainers have ruled that people no longer have to declare their LLM usage, as Torvalds himself calls a ban on AI "utterly stupid."

Submissions to the Linux kernel no longer require LLM generation declarations

It comes after a discussion from the Maintainers Summit

The first part of this story comes via a message sent to the Linux mailing list. It announces one of the major changes decided during the Maintainers Summit on October 8, 2026, in Prague, Czechia, where submissions to the kernel no longer need to use the "Assisted-by" tag:

"The Maintainers Summit reached consensus to deprecate the Assisted-by tag. Remove the documentation requiring it."

The "Assisted-by" tag was required if people used AI-generated content for their Linux kernel submissions. When writing the commit, the developer would write "Assisted-by: LLM [TOOL1] [TOOL2]," replacing the placeholders with their AI of choice. This new ruling by the Maintainers Summit removes that requirement, meaning that people can submit AI-generated code without needing to declare it as such.

GCC, the core compiler behind Linux, draws a hard line against AI code

No AI code here, thanks.

14
By  Simon Batt

Linus Torvalds calls the arguments against AI use "utterly stupid"

Any doubt about his stance on AI has surely been made known now

In some correspondence regarding concern about this new disclosure removal, the creator of Linux, Linus Torvalds, made his thoughts known. His statements come after someone claims that removal of these disclosures "is setting our expectations, telling what we want and what we don't want." Torvalds calls the issue a "hangup" and compares discussions around banning LLM submissions to a few hypotheticals:

"Here's a new rule just for you: don't use compilers for any of your kernel submissions.

Because if you can't show that you really understand what the machine is actually doing by writing your code in assembler, then I don't want to see your code contribution. You clearly aren't competent if you can't write it that way."

Torvalds then compares an AI ban to getting rid of text editors, as doing so would prove that someone could write a good commit message without making any mistakes.

He then rounds off his argument by asking, "Do you not see how UTTERLY STUPID those kinds of rules would be?" and stating that he simply expects the people working on the Linux kernel to "understand what they are doing." This aligns with his previous arguments for LLM-generated code, where he emphasises that people using AI code still need a solid foundation of knowledge when making use of this new technology.

Linus Torvalds will "loudly ignore" anyone criticising AI code in Linux: "Fork it. Or just walk away"

He has made his stance known.

4

item.title: I replaced Google search with a local LLM for a week, and it changed how I find answers
item.itunes:title: I replaced Google search with a local LLM for a week, and it changed how I find answers
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Searching with Google used to be the answer to everything. But these days, the answer sits somewhere below five sponsored results and an AI summary that's probably not accurate. Getting to the answer takes way more scrolling than the question actually deserves, and given user behavior, this usually means just settling for the easiest one, which might not be adequate.

Local LLMs have gotten good at answering questions without sending anything to big tech companies, and I also recently gave one filesystem access which ended up replacing Windows Search for the most part. But a model that fits on an 8GB GPU is usually a small one, and it only knows what it's trained on, which rules out recent and current events. So, I gave mine web access.

I stopped paying for ChatGPT after putting my local LLM on Tailscale

My phone finally reaches my home server the same way it reaches ChatGPT.

13
By  Korbin Brown

The problem with Google Search

Finding the answer feels like a treasure hunt now

Google search has been getting worse for years, and there's actual research behind that. A year-long study out of Germany tracked 7,392 product review searches across Google, Bing, and DuckDuckGo and found the top results were mostly pages built around affiliate links, and a good amount of it was just outright SEO spam. To be fair, the researchers said Google improved a bit over the year they watched it, though the average user probably wouldn't have noticed, and it was still riddled with spam at the end of the day.

And then there are the AI overviews; I have a love-hate relationship with them. They're insanely convenient, but at what cost? AI summaries often present personal opinions from forums as fact, so you have to verify all the information yourself anyway, and at that point you might as well keep scrolling like we used to before AI summaries. Plus, Google now runs ads inside the AI summaries too.

So it's not that Google search is completely useless, the vibe has simply changed and not for the better. Google decides what I see before I've even read anything. Most of the top of a results page is stuff Google wants in front of me, and not necessarily what I'm looking for.

I finally ditched Ollama after using llama.cpp's WebUI, and I'm not going back anytime soon

Using llama.cpp directly has never felt more polished

3
By  Samarveer Singh

Giving my local LLM the web

My local model can look things up without asking Google

A local model only knows what was in its training data. This is actually perfectly fine when you just want something explained or if the information you need to rely on is a few years old already. But anything recent will end up being a guess, for example, when I asked Gemma E4B what the date was, it confidently said 2016.

The fix is giving the model a way to look things up, and I ended up doing that in Jan, simply because it's the least annoying option. Setting up simply involves switching on a toggle in the settings and installing the Jan browser extension, rather than editing a config file. By default it searches through Exa on a free endpoint with no API key, which also means my questions weren't going through Google.

Search and fetch do different jobs - search gets the model a list of results with titles and short snippets, and fetch is the part that opens one of those pages and reads the actual text, otherwise the model is mostly working off snippets. Jan’s built-in web search gives the model both, so it can run a search and then pick a result to read on its own, and fetched pages get cut down to a set length before they reach the model so a single page doesn’t fill up its context.

LM Studio can do all of this as well, and I already have Brave Search set up in it, which is worth doing if you want an engine that runs its own index instead of borrowing from Google or Bing. It involves signing up for a Brave Search API and then editing the mcp.json file.

I tested every tiny local LLM worth running, and only three survived the cut

Small models are doing more than they should

1
By  Nolen Jonker

Letting a tiny model run my searches

My model now goes looking before it answers

On an 8GB card, picking your models will come down to whether it bothers to look things up at all. The Qwen family is very strong at tool calling, so I recommend picking something from there - my pick is Qwen 3.5 4B Q4_K_M for lighter chats and the 9B also at Q4_K_M for heavier work. Unlike Gemma, it uses search without having to be asked.

Once it does search, Jan makes the process pretty easy to follow. Qwen fetches the pages it wants to read and a little progress bar shows it working through them, which usually only takes seconds to complete. Jan also tells you which tool the model used, so you can tell whether it actually read a page or just went off the search snippets.

Searching didn't make Qwen 100% reliable though. When I asked what Obsidian released this month, it pulled ten sources and then dated the update October 2035. The heading under that said 2045, and the version number it gave me doesn't seem to exist anywhere. Most of those ten were third-party plugin changelogs, with only one coming from Obsidian itself, so I think it read a pile of loosely related pages and blended them together. But in its defense, my prompt was pretty vague; with Qwen you have to give more specifics to reel it in. Also, this is pretty much what the average AI summary looks like, anyway.

Jan lists the sources under every answer and you can open each one, so I'd go straight to the official page and check. The way it implements this feature is very user friendly - all your sources will be neatly stacked at the bottom.

Be mindful of context, though. One of my searches used 70% of my context window, and that was after I set Qwen to 30k context length! So if you're working with a smaller GPU, it's going to be about finding a balance between model, quant, context length, and the way you formulate your prompt. It might sound like hurdles, but it actually makes you more mindful about what to search for, which I feel is a lost art since AI entered the search engine game.

I finally found a local LLM I want to use every day (and it's not for coding)

Local AI that actually fits into my day

21
By  Nolen Jonker

A week of asking instead of searching

I still open Google, but just for different queries, such as going to an account login or finding hyper-specific real-time information like which restaurants are open near me right now. But questions start in my local LLM now, typed out properly. Now I just want to get this same setup on my phone, but that's a whole other story.

item.title: I finally found why my PC was waking from sleep for seemingly no reason
item.itunes:title: I finally found why my PC was waking from sleep for seemingly no reason
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Over the last few months, I had been dealing with a slightly annoying problem on my PC. Every few weeks, I walked in to see my PC running without any input from me. It seemed that the PC was waking up from sleep on a whim, and there didn't seem to be any pattern to it. As far as I knew, no one was moving my keyboard or mouse behind my back.

Upon further investigation, I found that a third-party app was scheduled to wake the PC up at regular intervals. This wasn't happening too frequently, so it had escaped my attention. If you're dealing with a similar issue, it doesn't have to be a scheduled task that's at fault; it could be a humble network packet or electrical interference.

3 reasons your PC sleeps or wakes at the wrong time

Look out for these if your PC is not obeying orders

By  Ali Tauseef

Scheduled tasks and wake timers were the culprits

I had forgotten about the schedule I had set up

As I mentioned, this "waking from sleep" problem wasn't that frequent, so it was easy to ignore it for a while. I use my PC regularly from morning through evening almost every day, so the errant wakes weren't that annoying. It was rare to find the PC running when I woke up in the morning, so even excess power consumption wasn't a huge concern.

That said, over two months, it finally got to me, so I had to find out what was wrong. One fine day, when I saw the PC had woken up from sleep, I finally opened an elevated Command Prompt and typed in "powercfg lastwake." It turned out that Macrium Reflect was the background process triggering the PC to wake up. The scheduled task was waking the PC up with a wake timer.

I had forgotten about the fortnightly backups that I had scheduled myself around two months ago, so I failed to connect the program to the seemingly unprompted wake-from-sleep events. On other occasions, it wasn't Macrium Reflect that was at fault; it was Windows Update. I had decided not to disable Windows Update (like I did on Windows 10) when I moved to Windows 11, so the OS was triggering infrequent wake-up events.

Stop trusting Windows sleep mode with your unsaved work

You might lose it all

3
By  João Carrasqueira

Wake-on-LAN might be accidentally waking your PC up

Or your network adapter settings may be suboptimal

While I found out that a third-party app and Windows Update were to blame in my case, your PC might have a different cause. In fact, Wake-on-LAN (WoL) is one of the most common reasons behind PCs waking from sleep. You may have installed a WoL app on your phone to wake the PC remotely when you need your Plex server online. If the app is located on your phone's home screen, triggering it accidentally is more common than you think.

Alternatively, your network adapter may be misconfigured to wake up on almost any network packet rather than a magic packet alone. Your router or mesh system can then wake your PC from sleep during status checks, client pings, or device discovery. It's uncommon, but it's known to happen. You can tweak the power properties of your network adapter in Device Manager to only allow magic packets to wake the PC.

4 reasons you might want to set up Wake-on-LAN on your PC

Wake-on-LAN can be a real time-saver.

7
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Your wireless peripherals might be the reason

Your keyboard and mouse are probably configured to wake your PC up

Lastly, the most boring reason might be true in your case: your wireless keyboard or mouse might be the triggers. I've configured my keyboard and mouse to wake the PC up on a keypress or mouse movement. However, my partner rarely uses my PC, and there's no one else who can accidentally trigger them. This might not be true in your case, since kids or pets can sometimes bump into your desk, instantly waking your PC from sleep.

The other potential cause is minor electrical interference triggering your wireless dongle just enough to be interpreted as actual user input. An AC, desk lamp, or other appliance turning on or off on the same circuit can send a tiny electrical surge toward your PC. These types of wake-from-sleep events are often hard to pin down, since most people don't connect them directly to their PC waking up.

4 reasons I'm never switching back to wired peripherals

Wired peripherals have their place, but I'm too far gone to switch back

36
By  Tanveer Singh

So, my PC wasn't waking up for no reason, after all

When my PC started waking from sleep at seemingly random intervals, I had assumed it was simply acting up. However, it turns out that Macrium Reflect and Windows Update were the triggers. You, too, can find out what's waking your PC from sleep, and it might not be a scheduled task or wake timer. Accidental peripheral movement or electrical interference can also be the culprits.

item.title: I thought I was done with live TV until I found this sketchy-looking free website
item.itunes:title: I thought I was done with live TV until I found this sketchy-looking free website
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I first started my career in journalism and blogging, I worked for a mainstream news publication where the TV was always on in the background, running a 24-hour news channel. While it helped the editorial team stay on top of the daily news grind, I appreciated the constant stream of information because it kept me connected to the world outside the tech industry bubble where I spend most of my time.

With that in mind, I recently decided to create a similar setup in my home office so I can better keep tabs on the news (I hear it's a dumpster fire out there). Sure, I could go to a national or local TV station's website and watch a livestream, but often I'm forced to create an account and sign in, or jump through hoops like downloading a dedicated app.

That's when I stumbled across Famelack (formerly TV Garden) in a Reddit post.

Famelack is a mostly legal, entirely free live TV directory

These channels are already available for free somewhere online

While the website's overall vibe reminds me of a pirated UFC or live sports streaming site (not that I'd ever watch something like that, of course), it's actually mostly legit to my understanding. The open-source project aggregates publicly available live TV streams from around the world. It pulls content from legitimate publicly available broadcasters, various YouTube livestreams, and IPTV directories. Many of these channels already stream online for free on different platforms, but Famelack puts them in one central place with a simple, easy-to-understand UI.

What's great is that when a stream goes offline or has an issue, Famelack pulls it down quickly. To be clear, the platform doesn't host or own any of the video content it links to. Instead, it's a directory that points you to streams already available elsewhere. This makes it vastly different from similar pirated stream-focused platforms.

Many of these are freely available OTA broadcasts or online streams you can find elsewhere, although some channels are typically associated with paid TV services, and it's not always clear whether the streams are authorized. Still, it's definitely not the same as someone ripping every episode of The Sopranos from HBO Max and streaming them on a platform called 42069b3ststreams, or something like that.

This app finally made my messy retro PC game port library effortless to manage

Quiver organized my growing old-school game recompilation collection perfectly.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

Have you ever wanted to watch the local news in Belize? Well, you can now

Welcome to worldwide live TV

Thankfully, Famelack doesn't bombard you with random torrent-site-level pop-ups. If you're seeing constant ads, you've accidentally landed on a website imitating Famelack's library (the TV Garden GitHub repository was archived back in January 2026). It's refreshing that, in this money-hungry world, Famelack is completely free of ads, as far as I can tell.

Since I'm Canadian, I typically want to watch CBC Toronto's broadcast, so I click on Canada on the spinning globe that's Famelack's interactive menu. Then I use the left-side menu to select the stream at the end of the list.

Famelack's quality isn't always the best, so if you're looking for a 4K stream, it's likely not the live TV platform for you. It might say the stream is 1080p, but the bitrate is often so low that on a large screen, everything looks potato-like (most streams let you set quality manually, thankfully). There's also a left-hand navigation menu with channel categories like Top News, Entertainment, Sports, and more, making it easy to find a specific live event if you're not sure which channel it's on.

The platform also supports picture-in-picture mode in Firefox and other browsers, letting me pop the stream out and drop it somewhere else on my two-monitor work setup. This makes low-resolution streams even less of an issue since the window size is so small. While I often see complaints that streams go down, the channels I watch have been pretty reliable, including various CBC regions, CP24, CTV, CNN, and occasionally Fox News, if I'm looking for a bit of comedic relief. Over the past few days of using Famelack, the only issue I've encountered is CNN going down a few times for a couple of minutes.

There's even a kind of fun randomizer mode that pulls up a random stream, though most of the time I can't even figure out what I'm watching. One time, a random, very odd Russian TV station appeared; another time, an entire channel dedicated to Wipeout showed up. I also sometimes take a break from work to load up a random stream from a random country, like Afghanistan's national news station.

Look, I'm not saying Famelack is a spectacular platform. It's passable at best, but for how I watch live TV — in a small window tucked into the corner of my monitor, usually on mute — it gets the job done.

The OLED screen and design improvements are great — it's just that the Z2 Extreme is showing its age.

item.title: I use Tailscale for everything now, and it's the most boring but incredible software I run
item.itunes:title: I use Tailscale for everything now, and it's the most boring but incredible software I run
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For years, I ignored the security of my home network. I knew better than to click on sketchy links or visit dodgy websites, so I figured it didn't matter. But now that I have gotten married and my wife and I entertain guests much more often than I used to, I've started to discover the cracks in the armor of my network. My entire network can be put at risk by a single guest with a malware-infected laptop, including well-meaning but clueless parents.

I started looking for a solution to keep my network and devices safe, even if I had guests who couldn't tell the difference between an ad and a scam. That's where Tailscale comes in. While it is, on the surface, a relatively boring application, it's one of the most useful tools I use daily. It has quickly become one of my favorite applications and has already proven its worth in protecting my network.

Setup couldn't be easier

No technical know-how required

There are numerous VPN options I could set up that would secure my network, but Tailscale simplifies the entire process. It uses WireGuard, and unlike the raw version, which requires manual configuration of cryptographic keys, Tailscale lets me log in with an existing account. In my case, I used my Google account, but Microsoft, GitHub, and others are also options. The Tailscale coordination server handles the setup for me; all I have to do is sign in with a device, and it finds any others on my account without any intervention on my part.

Beyond that, Tailscale also makes remote access safer. I can jump onto my home network when I'm out and about to check files on another machine without worry. It's also a great companion for remote streaming from my Jellyfin server, and that's a huge bonus now that I'm trying to shed as many streaming services as possible. Tailscale means I don't need to expose my Jellyfin connection to the broader internet.

Here's how I access all of my self-hosted services while I'm traveling

There are a lot of different ways to access your self-hosted services when away, but here's what works for me.

9
By  Adam Conway

Tailscale is mostly open source

I can verify its security myself

Tailscale is not completely open source. While major aspects of it include the WireGuard protocol, the core client, and certain client applications, its coordination servers are proprietary. However, enough of its code is open source that I can audit it myself and verify the application does what it claims. Since I'm basically trusting Tailscale with my entire home network, that's the level of reassurance I want in any security application. That said, I'm not likely to audit it myself; it's a huge undertaking, and I'm more likely to trust community audits than perform one myself.

Tailscale is a zero-trust model

Each connection is individually encrypted

Think of a traditional firewall like a castle wall. In many setups, if a device gains access beyond the firewall, it's trusted; after all, it wouldn't be there if it wasn't supposed to be. Tailscale doesn't work quite like that. Instead, it operates on the principle that every device must verify itself, like a high-security building with security checkpoints at every entrance. This means every connection is encrypted device-to-device, and it also means I have much more granular access control per device. With proper ACL configuration, I can ensure visitors can't access my other devices (although this is a more technical part of Tailscale than its default settings). Now, when guests connect to my Wi-Fi, they're on a different network than my own devices. My important machines are accessible only through Tailscale, which guests never use.

This also lends itself particularly well to smart home setups, as a compromised smart device is isolated and less likely to grant an attacker access to the rest of the network. Given the potential risks of a larger smart home configuration, especially one that uses devices with security flaws (like mine, as I test prototype devices regularly), the zero-trust model is a huge plus.

Tailscale is dependent on the company's coordination servers

The self-hosted alternative is significantly more technical

The ease of use of Tailscale relies on the company maintaining its coordination servers to keep everything running smoothly. If those servers go down, existing networks will still work (for a time, at least), but you wouldn't be able to link new devices. For some users, that's a deal-breaker; if you don't want to rely on a third-party and would prefer to keep everything in your own hands, there is a self-hosted version of Tailscale called Headscale, which allows you to provide your own coordination server. However, it requires a good deal more in the way of technical know-how.

Stop port forwarding your self-hosted services: Do this instead

Say goodbye to the hassles of port forwarding with this secure, easy-to-use alternative.

24
By  Dhruv Bhutani

The trade off is more than worth it

The simplicity is the driving factor

While relying on a third party isn't always ideal, as far as I'm concerned, it's absolutely worth it. The time it would take me to set up my own server, troubleshoot any issues that arose, and keep everything updated far exceeds the theoretical, infinitesimal risk of Tailscale suffering an infrastructure hiccup. The company is well-funded and has proven its reliability over the years. I'd rather spend 30 seconds setting up Tailscale than hours learning to configure Headscale; after all, my goal is network security. I don't plan to become a networking master. Besides that, convenience is why I've implemented proper network security instead of putting it off as I had for so long.

Tailscale is one of the easiest, most elegant options for home network security

The beauty of this application is that you don't need to be an expert to make it work. All you need to do is sign in on your devices, and you'll have the level of security you lacked before. There are more complicated options, of course, but cybersecurity is a lot like exercise: even a small amount is better than none at all, and implementing whatever tools work best for you is the way to go. It has become an invisible part of my network, but its effects are felt everywhere.

item.itunes:title: 5 things I 3D printed for my home lab that fixed problems I'd been living with
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I began my descent into the 3D printing ecosystem, I’d simply choose the coolest-looking STL files I could find online and have my filament-fed companion turn them into tangible models for my desk. But just like most enthusiasts, I quickly grew tired of vanity prints and began turning my attention to functional models that bore some practical utility. Kitchen and bathroom accessories were the first couple of models I created after pivoting to the functional side of 3D printing. But since I spend the majority of my time tinkering away in my home lab, I figured I could look into some cool models for my tech cave. And well, my 3D printer managed to get rid of some annoying problems plaguing my setup.

Cable cables, grommets, and clips

Without my 3D printer, my home lab would resemble a rat’s nest

Over the years, I’ve added all sorts of cool hardware to my home lab, and these range from cool server paraphernalia and recycled PCs to old tablets, random networking equipment, and even single-board computers. As you may have guessed, my army of devices requires a lot of power cords, with some needing Ethernet wires and additional I/O peripherals connected via cables.

Thanks to my 3D printer and OrcaSlicer, I was able to fine-tune several cable management tools for my home lab. Cable clips were the easiest ones to create, since I could just use the base models without any tweaks and stick them along the edge of my desk. Meanwhile, grommet STL files would often need some edits to fit around my makeshift racks, and the same holds true for the cable channels routing my wires around a corner of the floor.

Heck, I’ve even printed models to improve the cable management provisions within my server paraphernalia. Cable combs, for one, are a godsend for routing all the cables for the random motherboards I buy from flea markets. Since one of the cheap PC cases I bought for an X99 mobo doesn’t have a power shroud, I even printed a PSU shroud to hide the extra clutter from my semi-modular power supply.

My 3D printer pays for itself every time I skip buying a PC accessory

I've stopped buying small PC accessories because my 3D printer makes better ones

By  Ayush Pande

Mounts for network devices

Though I keep some of them on a rack, too

This one’s still a bit of a work in progress, since I keep most of my network equipment on a dedicated shelf. However, I’ve got a cheap 8-port switch that not only hooks up to my PVE cluster, but it’s also something I use to tinker with new machines and run benchmarks on my test bench.

Unfortunately, I was running out of desk real estate for this switch, and leaving it anywhere besides under the table would make it difficult to route the cables without making my setup a lot messier. But since I’ve got a 3D printer, I was able to print a mount for this switch – one that I’ve drilled into the wall behind the desk.

Single-board computer cases

And even microcontroller cases, for that matter

Remember how I said I’ve got a bunch of SBCs in my arsenal? Well, besides certain boards that ship with cases, most of my SBCs would remain scattered across my home lab without any form of protective casing whatsoever. Even if we remove the somewhat expensive price tags on Raspberry Pi cases, I’ve got plenty of obscure boards that don’t even have proper cases. So, I can’t even buy cases for them, especially since non-Raspberry Pi boards tend to have different interface layouts than their uber-popular counterparts.

Fortunately, the 3D printing community has created plenty of SBC models, and this includes STL files for non-mainstream boards. And for the tiny systems that are far too obscure, I can always tweak the STL files for typical Raspberry Pi cases to ensure that they’d fit my SBC arsenal. I’ve even built cases for a bunch of ESP32 modules that serve as DIY smart sensors for my Home Assistant hub.

USB device holder

They also house my microSD cards

Besides my server rigs and recycled hardware, I also use plenty of USB devices in my projects. There’s my USB flash drive, which includes a bunch of diagnosis and troubleshooting tools for Windows as well as Linux systems. Likewise, I’ve got a USB drive loaded with Ventoy, and I often update it with the latest ISOs of my favorite operating systems to ensure that I can still work on bare-metal experiments when the host PC doesn’t mesh well with PXE boot.

Then there are the wireless dongles for all the keyboards, mice, and controllers I’ve accumulated over the years. Without a dedicated container, I’d end up losing half of them within a month. As such, I’ve 3D printed a couple of containers for specific dongles, with the largest one featuring slots for the microSD cards I use with my SBCs.

Gridfinity drawers

For my tools, PCIe cards, and storage drives

Credit: 

Of course, with all the server paraphernalia, I’ve got a bunch of tools and spare PC components in my drawers. But despite my best efforts, it’s really hard to avoid turning my hardware-laden drawers into a mess, especially since I often swap components around for my server experiments.

The Gridfinity system single-handedly solved this issue, as it lets me create slots, bases, dividers, and a bunch of other prints to better organize my drawers. Better yet, tweaking the Gridfinity files is a lot easier via its generator, so I can have precisely-calibrated prints for my desks.

A 3D printer is a useful addition for home labs

Aside from all the prints I’ve listed so far, I’ve got a couple of other 3D models I’ve printed for my PCs. For example, I’ve got a headphone stand that also holds two additional controllers. Likewise, I’ve got a handrest made out of TPU, and this custom design works better than any paid options out there. Speaking of TPU, when I broke off a NAS leg while moving out of my apartment ages ago, I 3D printed a nearly identical one using this filament. And don’t even get me started on the different stands I’ve made for my laptops, keyboards, monitors, and tablets.

item.title: I've spent over $3,000 on ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, and only one was worth the money
item.itunes:title: I've spent over $3,000 on ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, and only one was worth the money
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Something I remember particularly well about the early days of generative AI is how quickly people developed an aversion to the idea of paying for yet another subscription. I could understand why! We were already paying monthly for everything from streaming services to cloud storage, and suddenly, using a chatbot just to draft a quick email or (unfortunately) write an essay was going to cost another $20 a month.

In fact, when ChatGPT Plus first launched in February 2023, Reddit was filled with people questioning whether a chatbot could possibly be worth that much. Fast forward a few years, and I've somehow managed to spend over $3,000 on subscriptions to ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini alone.

After spending that much money, I've come to realize that paying for an AI subscription isn't necessarily a waste of money. Paying for the wrong one, however, absolutely can be! So, here's the only one I'd happily continue paying for...

ChatGPT Plus is the easiest subscription to justify

OpenAI has finally won me over

If you'd told me six months ago that I'd be recommending a $20 ChatGPT Plus subscription over a $100 Claude Max subscription, I'd have looked you right in the eyes and laughed. However, over the last few weeks, ChatGPT has undeniably jumped to the very top of my list, and it's not even a particularly close competition anymore.

For starters, OpenAI's models have gotten significantly better. I've noticed the difference most when using Codex and Claude Code side by side, especially when giving both tools the exact same task. There was a time when Claude Code would consistently deliver better results, particularly when it came to building polished interfaces and figuring out what I wanted without needing me to spell out every little detail. Lately, though, the tables have turned. Codex has been doing a much better job of understanding my intentions, making sensible decisions on its own, and delivering finished products that actually feel finished.

Even when I preferred Claude for coding, I was always vocal about how ChatGPT still excelled as a general-purpose AI assistant. Whether I needed help researching a topic, understanding a complicated concept, brainstorming ideas, or simply figuring something out, ChatGPT was almost always the first tool I'd turn to. Now that Codex has caught up with, and in some cases surpassed, Claude Code in my own testing, I'm finding fewer and fewer reasons to pay for a separate Claude subscription.

The biggest reason, though, is the limits. Claude frankly has absurd usage limits, and I manage to hit my weekly limit just three days into the week! On the contrary, I can get through an entire week of using Codex on my $20 ChatGPT Plus subscription without running into nearly as many restrictions. Considering I was paying five times as much for Claude Max, it's becoming increasingly difficult to justify spending that kind of money when the cheaper alternative lets me get more work done.

Claude has lost the edge it once had

Oh, how the tables have turned

While I've already addressed most of the reasons I don't prefer Claude nearly as much as I used to, I think the biggest one is that it no longer has the unique edge that once made it so easy to recommend. It's not necessarily that Claude has gotten significantly worse. Rather, competing LLMs have caught up with, and in some cases surpassed, the things Claude used to do better than everyone else. And when that happens, all the little frustrations you've been willing to overlook suddenly become a lot harder to ignore.

I also feel like Anthropic has sort of slowed down in the last few months. I've always praised the company for staying ahead of the curve and introducing features that genuinely change how people use AI, rather than simply chasing whatever its competitors are doing. Lately, though, it feels like OpenAI has been moving at a much faster pace, rolling out new features and improvements that give me more reasons to keep coming back. That's not to say Claude has stopped improving, but for the first time in a long while, I find myself getting more excited about what OpenAI is doing than what Anthropic has up its sleeve.

Unfortunately, it's not just the pace of innovation that's been bothering me. A couple of months ago, I wrote an entire article about how exhausting Claude had become to use, particularly for research. Despite using its most capable model at the highest effort setting, I kept finding that Claude would rush through research tasks, overlook useful sources, or answer questions without even bothering to search the web.

In one experiment, I gave Claude and ChatGPT the exact same research question. Claude spent roughly a minute and a half putting together its answer, while ChatGPT spent around 12 minutes digging into the topic. The difference in the quality and depth of their responses was enough to make me question what I was paying so much more for.

Then there's the fact that Claude has occasionally taken it upon itself to decide how I should use my remaining allowance. I've had Claude Code discourage me from continuing a task because I was approaching my usage limit, even though I was perfectly happy to use whatever I had left. I understand warning users before they run out, but I don't think a tool I'm paying $100 a month for should be making that decision for me.

None of this means Claude is a bad AI assistant. Far from it! There are still things I prefer about Claude, and I wouldn't hesitate to recommend trying it. But recommending Claude and recommending a paid Claude subscription are two very different things. With the competition getting better and the frustrations piling up, I just don't see enough reasons to keep paying for Claude Max anymore.

Gemini is the weakest reason to pay for Google AI Pro

Everything but the chatbot makes it worthwhile

Google AI Pro is a slightly different story. Unlike ChatGPT Plus and Claude Pro, where the main selling point is access to better AI models and higher usage limits, Google's subscription comes bundled with a bunch of other perks that make it surprisingly easy to justify.

For instance, I use NotebookLM practically every day for studying, and I genuinely wouldn't hesitate to pay $20 a month for its premium features alone. The higher limits are incredibly useful, especially when I'm working with multiple lectures, readings, and presentations. So, the fact that Google AI Pro includes an upgraded NotebookLM experience alongside 5TB of cloud storage, Gemini integrations across Google's productivity apps, and access to other tools like Flow and Antigravity makes it a pretty compelling package.

There's even YouTube Premium Lite included in select countries, which is a nice bonus if you're someone who spends a ridiculous amount of time watching YouTube. And if you already rely heavily on Gmail, Google Docs, and Drive, I can absolutely see Google AI Pro being the subscription that makes the most financial sense for you.

The problem, at least for me, is Gemini itself. While Google's models have certainly improved, I still find myself turning to ChatGPT or Claude for most of the things I'd normally use a general-purpose AI assistant for. Whether it's brainstorming ideas, researching something, or tackling a complicated task, Gemini rarely ends up being my first choice.

I tried replacing Claude with Gemini, ChatGPT, and Perplexity for a month – here's the only one worth paying for

Three tools, one winner

19
By  Parth Shah

In every comparison where I've pitted Codex, Claude Code, and Antigravity against each other, Antigravity has, without fail, been the one that disappointed me the most. It's not necessarily that it can't get the job done, but the results often feel far less polished than what its competitors deliver. I've had instances where Antigravity declared a project finished despite leaving out features I'd explicitly requested, and others where I had to step in to fix problems that ideally should've been caught during testing.

That's ultimately why I find Google AI Pro a little difficult to recommend purely for Gemini. The subscription itself offers tremendous value, particularly if you're already invested in Google's ecosystem, but I don't think the chatbot or coding experience alone is compelling enough to make me choose it over ChatGPT Plus.

So, all that to say, the subscription I can most easily recommend right now is ChatGPT Plus. Claude would be my next pick if you're looking for an AI assistant primarily for writing or coding, though I'd think twice before splurging on its more expensive tiers. I'd only recommend Google AI Pro if the AI itself isn't your main reason for subscribing, and you're more interested in perks like NotebookLM, cloud storage, and integrations with Google's other services.

Something I remember particularly well about the early days of generative AI is how quickly people developed an aversion to the idea of paying for yet another subscription. I could understand why! We were already paying monthly for everything from streaming services to cloud storage, and suddenly, using a chatbot just to draft a quick email or (unfortunately) write an essay was going to cost another $20 a month.

In fact, when ChatGPT Plus first launched in February 2023, Reddit was filled with people questioning whether a chatbot could possibly be worth that much. Fast forward a few years, and I've somehow managed to spend over $3,000 on subscriptions to ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini alone.

After spending that much money, I've come to realize that paying for an AI subscription isn't necessarily a waste of money. Paying for the wrong one, however, absolutely can be! So, here's the only one I'd happily continue paying for...

ChatGPT Plus is the easiest subscription to justify

OpenAI has finally won me over

If you'd told me six months ago that I'd be recommending a $20 ChatGPT Plus subscription over a $100 Claude Max subscription, I'd have looked you right in the eyes and laughed. However, over the last few weeks, ChatGPT has undeniably jumped to the very top of my list, and it's not even a particularly close competition anymore.

For starters, OpenAI's models have gotten significantly better. I've noticed the difference most when using Codex and Claude Code side by side, especially when giving both tools the exact same task. There was a time when Claude Code would consistently deliver better results, particularly when it came to building polished interfaces and figuring out what I wanted without needing me to spell out every little detail. Lately, though, the tables have turned. Codex has been doing a much better job of understanding my intentions, making sensible decisions on its own, and delivering finished products that actually feel finished.

Even when I preferred Claude for coding, I was always vocal about how ChatGPT still excelled as a general-purpose AI assistant. Whether I needed help researching a topic, understanding a complicated concept, brainstorming ideas, or simply figuring something out, ChatGPT was almost always the first tool I'd turn to. Now that Codex has caught up with, and in some cases surpassed, Claude Code in my own testing, I'm finding fewer and fewer reasons to pay for a separate Claude subscription.

The biggest reason, though, is the limits. Claude frankly has absurd usage limits, and I manage to hit my weekly limit just three days into the week! On the contrary, I can get through an entire week of using Codex on my $20 ChatGPT Plus subscription without running into nearly as many restrictions. Considering I was paying five times as much for Claude Max, it's becoming increasingly difficult to justify spending that kind of money when the cheaper alternative lets me get more work done.

Claude has lost the edge it once had

Oh, how the tables have turned

While I've already addressed most of the reasons I don't prefer Claude nearly as much as I used to, I think the biggest one is that it no longer has the unique edge that once made it so easy to recommend. It's not necessarily that Claude has gotten significantly worse. Rather, competing LLMs have caught up with, and in some cases surpassed, the things Claude used to do better than everyone else. And when that happens, all the little frustrations you've been willing to overlook suddenly become a lot harder to ignore.

I also feel like Anthropic has sort of slowed down in the last few months. I've always praised the company for staying ahead of the curve and introducing features that genuinely change how people use AI, rather than simply chasing whatever its competitors are doing. Lately, though, it feels like OpenAI has been moving at a much faster pace, rolling out new features and improvements that give me more reasons to keep coming back. That's not to say Claude has stopped improving, but for the first time in a long while, I find myself getting more excited about what OpenAI is doing than what Anthropic has up its sleeve.

Unfortunately, it's not just the pace of innovation that's been bothering me. A couple of months ago, I wrote an entire article about how exhausting Claude had become to use, particularly for research. Despite using its most capable model at the highest effort setting, I kept finding that Claude would rush through research tasks, overlook useful sources, or answer questions without even bothering to search the web.

In one experiment, I gave Claude and ChatGPT the exact same research question. Claude spent roughly a minute and a half putting together its answer, while ChatGPT spent around 12 minutes digging into the topic. The difference in the quality and depth of their responses was enough to make me question what I was paying so much more for.

Then there's the fact that Claude has occasionally taken it upon itself to decide how I should use my remaining allowance. I've had Claude Code discourage me from continuing a task because I was approaching my usage limit, even though I was perfectly happy to use whatever I had left. I understand warning users before they run out, but I don't think a tool I'm paying $100 a month for should be making that decision for me.

None of this means Claude is a bad AI assistant. Far from it! There are still things I prefer about Claude, and I wouldn't hesitate to recommend trying it. But recommending Claude and recommending a paid Claude subscription are two very different things. With the competition getting better and the frustrations piling up, I just don't see enough reasons to keep paying for Claude Max anymore.

Gemini is the weakest reason to pay for Google AI Pro

Everything but the chatbot makes it worthwhile

Google AI Pro is a slightly different story. Unlike ChatGPT Plus and Claude Pro, where the main selling point is access to better AI models and higher usage limits, Google's subscription comes bundled with a bunch of other perks that make it surprisingly easy to justify.

For instance, I use NotebookLM practically every day for studying, and I genuinely wouldn't hesitate to pay $20 a month for its premium features alone. The higher limits are incredibly useful, especially when I'm working with multiple lectures, readings, and presentations. So, the fact that Google AI Pro includes an upgraded NotebookLM experience alongside 5TB of cloud storage, Gemini integrations across Google's productivity apps, and access to other tools like Flow and Antigravity makes it a pretty compelling package.

There's even YouTube Premium Lite included in select countries, which is a nice bonus if you're someone who spends a ridiculous amount of time watching YouTube. And if you already rely heavily on Gmail, Google Docs, and Drive, I can absolutely see Google AI Pro being the subscription that makes the most financial sense for you.

The problem, at least for me, is Gemini itself. While Google's models have certainly improved, I still find myself turning to ChatGPT or Claude for most of the things I'd normally use a general-purpose AI assistant for. Whether it's brainstorming ideas, researching something, or tackling a complicated task, Gemini rarely ends up being my first choice.

I tried replacing Claude with Gemini, ChatGPT, and Perplexity for a month – here's the only one worth paying for

Three tools, one winner

19
By  Parth Shah

In every comparison where I've pitted Codex, Claude Code, and Antigravity against each other, Antigravity has, without fail, been the one that disappointed me the most. It's not necessarily that it can't get the job done, but the results often feel far less polished than what its competitors deliver. I've had instances where Antigravity declared a project finished despite leaving out features I'd explicitly requested, and others where I had to step in to fix problems that ideally should've been caught during testing.

That's ultimately why I find Google AI Pro a little difficult to recommend purely for Gemini. The subscription itself offers tremendous value, particularly if you're already invested in Google's ecosystem, but I don't think the chatbot or coding experience alone is compelling enough to make me choose it over ChatGPT Plus.

So, all that to say, the subscription I can most easily recommend right now is ChatGPT Plus. Claude would be my next pick if you're looking for an AI assistant primarily for writing or coding, though I'd think twice before splurging on its more expensive tiers. I'd only recommend Google AI Pro if the AI itself isn't your main reason for subscribing, and you're more interested in perks like NotebookLM, cloud storage, and integrations with Google's other services.
